title: Normalization and Normal Forms
relevance: Interviewers use normalization to test whether candidates can spot redundancy, anomalies, and functional-dependency violations when designing or reviewing relational schemas.

phases.goal: Establish what normalization is, why unnormalized designs fail, and the definition of each normal form from 1NF through 5NF.

must_hit.point: Normalization decomposes a table into multiple related tables to remove redundancy while keeping the decomposition lossless.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states decomposition for less redundancy plus the lossless requirement, not just 'split tables'.

must_hit.point: Unnormalized designs suffer insertion, deletion, and updation anomalies that corrupt integrity.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all three anomaly types and briefly distinguishes add-without-unrelated-data, delete-losing-independent-facts, and multi-row update inconsistency.

must_hit.point: 1NF (E.F. Codd) requires every cell atomic: no multivalued or composite attributes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says one value per cell / no lists-in-a-cell, optionally citing Codd.

must_hit.point: 2NF requires 1NF and no partial dependency: every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole candidate key.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links 1NF plus 'no non-prime on a proper subset of a CK'.

must_hit.point: 3NF requires 2NF and no transitive dependency of a non-prime on the CK; equivalently for every FD X→Y, X is a superkey or Y is prime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives either the transitive-dependency wording or the superkey-or-prime test.

must_hit.point: BCNF requires every non-trivial FD X→Y to have X as a superkey; BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States LHS-must-be-superkey and the strict containment hierarchy.

must_hit.point: 4NF is BCNF with no non-trivial multivalued dependency; 5NF (PJNF) is 4NF with no non-trivial join dependency.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions MVD for 4NF and join dependency / Project-Join Normal Form for 5NF.

probes: What is normalization, and what three anomalies does a single wide Student–Course–Faculty table create?
Define 1NF through BCNF, and how does the containment hierarchy look?

hints.1: Start from why one wide table is bad, then layer forms as successive FD restrictions.
hints.2: Map anomalies → atomic cells (1NF) → no partial FD (2NF) → no transitive FD (3NF) → every LHS superkey (BCNF).
hints.3: Normalization = lossless decomposition to cut redundancy; anomalies are insert/delete/update; BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF.

phases.goal: Show how to detect partial/transitive FDs, run the 3NF vs BCNF tests, and check lossless and dependency-preserving decompositions including MVDs.

must_hit.point: Partial dependency example: CK={CustomerID,StoreID}, StoreID→Location with Location non-prime violates 2NF; fix by Store(StoreID, Location).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Identifies StoreID as proper subset of CK determining Location and names the split.

must_hit.point: On R(A,B,C,D,E,F) with FDs {CD→F, E→A, EC→D, A→B}, CK={EC} via EC⁺ covering all attributes; E→A is a partial dependency so not 2NF.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Finds CK={EC}, primes {E,C}, non-primes {A,B,D,F}, flags E→A.

must_hit.point: Transitive example Rollno→State→City fails 3NF because State→City has State not a superkey and City not prime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Applies the equivalent 3NF test to State→City and both conditions fail.

must_hit.point: R(A,B,C,D) with AB→CD and D→A has CK={AB,BD}; D→A passes 3NF (A prime) but fails BCNF (D not superkey).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States overlapping CKs, 3NF yes because A is prime, BCNF no because LHS D is not a superkey.

must_hit.point: Decomposition R→R1,R2 is lossless iff R1∩R2 is a superkey of R1 or R2; else the natural join can invent spurious tuples.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the intersection-superkey rule and links failure to spurious tuples.

must_hit.point: Dependency-preserving means the union of projected FDs on fragments implies the original F⁺.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says projected FDs together recover F⁺, not merely that tables still join.

must_hit.point: A non-trivial MVD A→→B needs at least 3 columns, the MVD, and B independent of the other attribute(s); Enrolment(s_id,course,hobby) with independent course/hobby violates 4NF and splits into CourseOpted and Hobbies.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the three MVD conditions and the two-table fix for independent course/hobby.

probes: Given CK={CustomerID,StoreID} and StoreID→Location, why is that not 2NF and how do you fix it?
When does a decomposition stay lossless, and how can a relation be in 3NF but not BCNF?

hints.1: Classify attributes as prime vs non-prime before hunting partial or transitive FDs.
hints.2: For BCNF vs 3NF, check whether the RHS being prime can rescue 3NF when the LHS is not a key.
hints.3: Lossless ⇔ common attributes form a superkey of one side; classic 3NF-not-BCNF is AB→CD with D→A and CKs {AB,BD}.

phases.goal: Contrast what 3NF vs BCNF decompositions guarantee about losslessness and dependency preservation.

must_hit.point: A 3NF decomposition can always be both lossless and dependency-preserving.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the always-both guarantee for 3NF.

must_hit.point: A BCNF decomposition is always lossless but may not be dependency-preserving.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts always-lossless BCNF with possible loss of FD enforcement across fragments.

must_hit.point: In the AB→CD, D→A example, BCNF fragments that separate A from B can make AB→C impossible to enforce inside one fragment.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Connects splitting DA away from B with inability to preserve AB→C locally.

probes: If you must choose between a 3NF design and a BCNF design, what do you gain and risk on dependency preservation?
Why might enforcing BCNF force you to give up a functional dependency you still need?

hints.1: Compare the two guarantees side by side: lossless vs dependency-preserving.
hints.2: Recall that BCNF is stricter on determinants, so splitting keys can scatter a composite FD.
hints.3: 3NF can always be lossless+DP; BCNF always lossless but may lose DP—e.g. AB→CD with D→A when A and B land in different fragments.

phases.goal: Apply highest-normal-form analysis to schema variants the way an OA or GATE-style question would.

must_hit.point: Highest-NF workflow: find CKs and primes, then test 2NF (no partial), 3NF (RHS prime if LHS not SK), BCNF (LHS CK/SK), stopping at the first failure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes iterative strongest-to-weaker checking from keys outward.

must_hit.point: GATE-2018 S1 Registration(rollno,courseid) with only the composite key's trivial FDs is in BCNF.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says BCNF because no non-trivial FD beyond the key.

must_hit.point: GATE-2018 S2 Registration(rollno,courseid,email) with email→rollno is BCNF because email is also a candidate key so every determinant is a key.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Treats email as CK alongside the registration key and concludes BCNF.

must_hit.point: GATE-2018 S3 Registration(rollno,courseid,marks,grade) with marks→grade is only 2NF: transitive dependency between non-primes fails 3NF.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Flags marks→grade as transitive non-prime→non-prime and answers 2NF.

must_hit.point: GATE-2018 S4 Registration(rollno,courseid,credit) with courseid→credit is only 1NF: courseid is a proper subset of CK determining a non-prime (partial dependency).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names partial dependency on courseid and answers 1NF.

probes: For Registration(rollno, courseid, marks, grade) with marks→grade, what is the highest normal form and why?
Walk the four GATE-2018 Registration variants and state highest NF for each.

hints.1: First write the candidate key for Registration, then see what each extra attribute depends on.
hints.2: Partial (subset of CK→non-prime) caps at 1NF; transitive non-prime→non-prime caps at 2NF; all determinants keys ⇒ BCNF.
hints.3: S1/S2 BCNF; S3 marks→grade ⇒ 2NF only; S4 courseid→credit ⇒ 1NF only.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: 3NF can always be decomposed to be both lossless and dependency-preserving. BCNF decomposition is always lossless but may fail dependency preservation—illustrated when AB→CD and D→A force fragments that separate A from B and lose local enforcement of AB→C.

tradeoffs.topic: Staying in 3NF vs pushing to BCNF with overlapping candidate keys
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Overlapping keys can make D→A legal in 3NF because A is prime even though D is not a superkey; BCNF still rejects that FD. Choosing BCNF removes that anomaly at the risk of losing dependency preservation.

gotchas.trap: Assuming every relation in 3NF is automatically in BCNF.
gotchas.correction: A relation can pass 3NF yet fail BCNF when overlapping candidate keys exist—e.g. R(A,B,C,D) with AB→CD and D→A: D→A is allowed in 3NF because A is prime, but BCNF requires D to be a superkey.

gotchas.trap: Treating any common attribute between R1 and R2 as enough for a safe split.
gotchas.correction: Lossless join requires R1∩R2 to be a superkey of R1 or R2; if not (as when splitting R(ABC) into AB and BC with non-key B), the join invents spurious tuples.

gotchas.trap: Thinking BCNF decomposition always preserves all original FDs the way 3NF can.
gotchas.correction: BCNF guarantees losslessness only; dependency preservation may fail, unlike 3NF which can always achieve both.

gotchas.trap: Storing independent multi-valued facts (course and hobby) in one Enrolment table and calling it fine because it is in BCNF-looking shape.
gotchas.correction: Independent MVDs (s_id→→course and s_id→→hobby) violate 4NF and cause a Cartesian blow-up; decompose into separate two-column tables such as CourseOpted and Hobbies.
